https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: Pedro Sánchez accused his opponents of hurling insults and lies but his conservative rival has promised a new era of politics
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's PP holds a narrow lead in the opinion polls

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
Abascal said on Friday that Sánchez's government had 'betrayed' Spaniards

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.

All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820: Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3pw: Weary of war but with no sign of backing down, Kyiv faces another punishing winter

Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.
Kyiv is entering its fourth winter following Russia's full-scale invasion

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckd7: Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.
Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.
“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions.
"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."
The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars

Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rr: The French president said he was proud to have led efforts to ban Brazilian meat products
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.

In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.
Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.
Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".
Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel which capsized off the holiday island of Ibiza on Thursday will be towed to the port of Cartagena, officials in Spain say.
All 17 of the Malta-registered Med Emre's crew members were rescued but the chief engineer later died in hospital. Six people were treated for minor injuries.
There had been concerns of a major oil spillage in the western Mediterranean but an inspection showed that the ship's fuel tanks are intact. An investigation is under way into what happened.
The vessel had been travelling from Algeciras near Gibraltar to Barcelona and is expected to arrive in Cartagena on Monday in what is being seen as a challenging rescue operation.

In a statement on Friday, the Spanish transport ministry said the tanker would be towed to Cartagena "as it is the only one [port] that meets the technical requirements to carry out cargo extraction and repair work".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez told Cadena SER radio network he hoped the tanker could be taken to port "in the coming hours, in the coming days".
"The information suggests that, indeed... this leak is not happening", he added.
The Spanish authorities provided no details about how the diesel would be extracted.
Meanwhile, pictures have emerged showing emergency workers inspecting the tanker's hull.
Any possible environmental damage is being assessed by air and pollution control vessel Clara Campoamor, which is owned by Spain's national maritime rescue service.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of the port of Valencia, earlier told news agency AFP that a small slick which had formed around the vessel had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk as originally reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call late on Wednesday, according to Spanish media.
Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle. It capsized in the early hours on Thursday.

Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline, in the country's north-west.
More than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil spilled into the sea.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4: The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves
A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.
Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing.
The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.
assault causing actual bodily harm and five counts of cruelty to a child
being in possession of an article connected with an offence under Kenya's Prevention of Terrorism Act, 2012.
Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.
Stephen Mwiti, who lost six children to the cult, welcomed the conviction of Mackenzie for murder last month
When the shallow graves were discovered, local men were hired for the horrifying task of exhuming the remains.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq3d: Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.

Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.

"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckr5: Tame says her "whole body was prickling with distress" over what Handbury said.
An Australian former media executive has admitted he said a child sex abuse survivor and prominent advocate "must be looking to be raped again" because of the way she was dressed at an event.
Grace Tame, 31, was groomed and abused by a teacher and has been honoured as Australian of the Year in 2021 for her advocacy work on child safety.
In an op-ed for independent media outlet Crikey, Tame said she overheard Matt Handbury speaking to a friend, and was left distressed by the remark and the failure of others who heard it to intervene.

Handbury, nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms, has not responded to a BBC request for comment, but in an email to Tame said he regretted the "highly objectionable" comment as soon as he said it.
Matt Handbury is the nephew of Rupert Murdoch and a former executive at his firms
Tame wrote in the Crikey article that she confronted Handbury - who she hadn't met before - immediately, and again later in the evening to check she had heard him correctly.
She said the encounter at the University of New South Wales event last week triggered flashbacks to her abuse and left her feeling like she would vomit.
"My whole body was prickling in distress," she wrote for Crikey.

"The many men and women who'd seen the confrontation were incredulous, and quick to express their anger at Matt's behaviour... Ironically though, in a room full of seasoned activists, journalists, lawyers and actual whistleblowers, not one person besides me took Matt to task in the heat of the moment."
The next day, in an email seen by the BBC, Handbury, 77, apologised for the "attempt at humour in less than poor taste".
"I did make reference to your strikingly attractive get-up... I also said: 'She must be looking to be raped again.'
He thanked her for "calling me out" and "opening my eyes more fully to this flaw in my nature which I will certainly be discussing with my very non-misogynist shrink".
"But no-one can deny you looked absolutely fabulous last night," he said, before signing off.
Handbury ran Murdoch Magazines for 13 years after buying the business from his uncle in 1991. He sold it to Seven Network's subsidiary Pacific Publications in 2004.
Tame said Handbury's remarks were "especially egregious" because it referenced a "very real, criminally tested traumatic experience, which he knew about" rather than an "imagined harm".
"It swiftly reawakened deep-seated physical wounds and haunting memories. How is that funny?"

From the age of 15, Tame was groomed and raped by her 58-year-old maths teacher Nicolaas Ockert Bester. He was later found guilty and served one year and nine months in jail for sexually abusing Tame when she was his student in 2011.
"They're not always as extreme, public or evidenced, but these kinds of experiences are part of my everyday life," Tame wrote on Instagram of Handbury's remarks.
"I'm tired of the maltreatment; and the gaslighting that follows. Tired of being provoked, then asked why I'm angry.
"I'm tired of copping more flak for fighting injustice than those who mete it out."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French President Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.

Uefa says it has appointed ethics and disciplinary inspectors "to conduct investigations into the incidents and examine all available evidence" from the Marseille-Levski Sofia and Besiktas-Hapoel Be'er-Sheva games.
European football's governing body said it "strongly condemns the serious incidents of violence and disorder" at those ties.
It added: "Violence, aggression, hatred and any form of provocative, discriminatory or extremist behaviour have no place in football.
"Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety."

In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."

Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Police response to Besiktas fans' pro-Palestine banner 'unacceptable'
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".

Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Besiktas fans clash with Georgian police at their game against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva

Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: An official holds one of the seized Vallarta mud turtles - they are now receiving care at a specialised sanctuary
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.
The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.
The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.
It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.
The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.
Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.
In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.
They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.
Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.
In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles , external that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.
Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases , external . Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c69q: Gianni De Gennaro worked in the anti-mafia directorate and became police chief before he headed Italian defence company Finmeccanica, later renamed Leonardo
Italian ex-police chief Gianni De Gennaro has denied misleading investigations into high-profile Mafia killings, in a letter written shortly before his death.
His body was found at his Tuscan country home on Saturday and Italian authorities believe he took his own life. A post mortem examination was due to take place on Friday.
In his eight-page note, De Gennaro, 78, vehemently denied obstructing the inquiry into the murder of anti-mafia judge Paolo Borsellino in Sicily in July 1992.
The Cosa Nostra Mafia was found to have ordered Borsellino's killing and that of fellow judge Giovanni Falcone two months earlier.
But several fruitless investigations were later launched into potential cover-ups by high-ranking officials.
In a recent inquiry De Gennaro, who in the 1990s worked in the anti-mafia directorate and later became Italy's police chief, was accused of misdirecting the initial investigation.
The allegations shocked many Italians, as De Gennaro had worked closely with Falcone and was seen as being on the front line of the fight against organised crime.

"In a few minutes I will be gone, so you understand well that a 'man condemned to death' cannot lie," he wrote in the letter, published by Italian daily Corriere della Sera. "I have never betrayed my oath of loyalty to the Fatherland."
Gianni De Gennaro (L) and anti-mafia judge Giovanni Falcone in 1992
"I hope that, amid the avalanche of falsehoods now overwhelming me, the truth will ultimately prevail," he added.
The case, and the media furore that has surrounded it, have re-opened the wound of the Mafia killings of the early 1990s, which remain an emotionally charged issue in Italy.
The story has dominated Italian headlines since De Gennaro's death, with several of the country's most senior political figures publicly commenting on the case.
On Thursday Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she had been "deeply shocked" by the case.
"His words struck us deeply, and I think the most important think we can do now is to help prosecutors who are working to clear things up," she added.
The letter was found next to a hard drive which he said contained notes from his 40-year career.

According to Italian media, investigators seized two hard drives, one from the home of De Gennaro's son and one from a former member of his security detail, and two USB sticks held by a close collaborator, who is also under investigation.
The sticks are reportedly labelled "Stato-Mafia", a likely reference to the alleged relationship between the Italian state and the Mafia, and "Massacres".
Forensic specialists are now expected to examine whether any files on the hard drives or USB sticks were altered or deleted, reports say.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07: Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be " excessively harsh ".
India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: It is rare for such a high-ranking official to face public criminal trials in Kenya
A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, along with two former aides, over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about".
Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.
His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.
The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.
Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.
She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.
A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.
Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.
On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.
Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo, told Kenya's Daily Nation that they would file an appeal seeking Obado's acquittal.
Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.
He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck05: Patterson was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives
Australia's mushroom killer Erin Patterson has launched a final legal bid to overturn her murder convictions and avoid dying in jail.
Patterson, 52, was last year found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023.

Last month, in Victoria's Court of Appeal three judges dismissed an appeal against her convictions and threw out the possibility she could be released on parole – saying her crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms".
She has now made a last-ditch application to the High Court to look at her case.
Patterson had 28 days to file an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court, a deadline which expired on Friday.
She wants the country's top judges to examine both her conviction and sentence - but the court does not have to agree to look at the case. It only hears appeals in about 10% of cases.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms which she had tracked down, foraged and prepared.
Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.
He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face. This glimmer of hope of freedom was thrown out by the appeal judges, who ruled she should never be released.
She had argued her conviction was unsafe on seven grounds - including a hotel booking mix up which saw the jury stay in the same place as the prosecution, a key police witness and the media.
Her lawyers said this was "catastrophic" and undermined the integrity of her trial, but the appeal court judges dismissed all the grounds for appeal.
